title: "Performance & Anti-patterns"
subtitle: "≈ “vectorise, don't loop” · data.table habits"
jupyter: python3
---

Polars is fast when Rust does the work and slow whenever Python does it a
row, a group or a piece at a time. This chapter measures the habits that
cross into Python, what chunks and sorted flags change, where the threads
go, and how to time a query now that `profile()` is gone. Linked, not
repeated: the UDF ladder
([Programming](../program/programming.qmd#sec-prog-udf)), the optimizer and a
measured eager-vs-lazy query ([Lazy API](lazy.qmd#sec-lazy-measured)),
memory and dtype shrinking ([Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-recipes)),
String vs Enum speed ([Categorical](../types/categorical.qmd#sec-cat-why)).

## In tidyverse {#sec-perf-tidyverse}

```r
# Loop vs vectorised: rows, groups, pieces
for (i in seq_len(nrow(flights))) flights$mph[i] <- flights$distance[i] / flights$air_time[i] * 60
flights |> mutate(mph = distance / air_time * 60)
flights |> group_split(tailnum) |>
  map(\(d) summarise(d, delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE), .by = tailnum)) |> list_rbind()
flights |> summarise(delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE), .by = tailnum)
out <- NULL; for (f in files) out <- rbind(out, read.csv(f))   # copies everything, every time
out <- files |> map(read_csv) |> list_rbind()

# data.table habits
DT[, mph := distance / air_time * 60]; setkey(DT, time_hour); setDTthreads(4)
DT[, mean(dep_delay), by = tailnum, verbose = TRUE]   # GForce: internal C per group
```

The folklore carries over, for a different reason. An R loop is slow because
each iteration is interpreted and `df$x[i] <-` copies on modify; a Polars loop
is slow because each iteration leaves Rust, builds Python objects, and comes
back. data.table habits map like this:

| data.table | Polars | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `DT[, x := f(y)]` (by reference) | `df.with_columns(x=...)` | a new frame, but untouched columns are shared ([Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-sharing)) |
| `setkey(DT, t)` | `df.sort("t")` | sorts and sets the sorted flag (@sec-perf-sorted) |
| `setattr(DT, "sorted", "t")` | `pl.col("t").set_sorted()` | a promise, not a check (@sec-perf-sorted-lie) |
| `rbindlist(list_of_dts)` | `pl.concat(list_of_dfs)` | once, not in a loop (@sec-perf-grow) |
| GForce `mean(x)` by group | a native expression in `agg()` | a Python function in `agg()` is the slow path |
| `setDTthreads(n)` | `POLARS_MAX_THREADS=n`, before import | @sec-perf-threads |
| `verbose = TRUE` | `pl.Config.set_verbose()`, `POLARS_LOG_METRICS=1` | @sec-perf-profile |
| `bench::mark()` | `%timeit`, or `race()` below | @sec-perf-bench |

: data.table habits → Polars {.striped}

## Mental model {#sec-perf-model}

```text
 native expression     Python: build the Expr once ──► Rust: one compiled pass over n rows
                       cost ≈ n × nanoseconds

 Python loop           Python ──┬── iteration 1 ──► Rust ──► Python objects
                                ├── iteration 2 ──► Rust ──► Python objects
                                └── … × k   (k = rows, groups or pieces)
                       cost ≈ k × microseconds, plus one Python object per value

 a Series in memory    [chunk 0][chunk 1][chunk 2] …   a list of Arrow buffers
                       concat / vstack append pointers (no copy); rechunk() copies into one
```

- **Count crossings, not rows.** A loop over 3 groups is harmless; over 4,044
  groups it is not; over 336,776 rows it never is.
- **Chunks are cheap to make and costly to iterate.** A handful is normal;
  thousands slow every element-wise step that follows.
- **Metadata lets Polars skip work, and Polars believes it.** A sorted flag
  turns `sort()` and `max()` into lookups, and a false one into wrong answers.

## Mechanics {#sec-perf-mechanics}

```{python}
#| include: false
%xmode Minimal
```

```{python}
import json
import os
import re
import statistics
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import timeit
from collections.abc import Callable

import pandas as pd
import polars as pl
from polars.testing import assert_frame_equal
from pl_notes import datasets

flights_df = datasets.flights()
```

### Measuring fairly {#sec-perf-bench}

```{python}
def bench(f: Callable[[], object], runs: int = 5) -> float:
    """Median wall time of f() in ms, after one untimed warm-up call."""
    f()
    return statistics.median(timeit.repeat(f, number=1, repeat=runs)) * 1000


def race(candidates: dict[str, Callable[[], object]], runs: int = 5) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """≈ bench::mark() without the result check: median ms, and ratio to the fastest."""
    ms = {name: bench(f, runs) for name, f in candidates.items()}
    return pl.DataFrame({"approach": list(ms), "ms": list(ms.values())}).with_columns(
        pl.col("ms").round(2), x_fastest=(pl.col("ms") / pl.col("ms").min()).round(1)
    )
```

`timeit` uses `time.perf_counter()` and pauses garbage collection while it
times. The warm-up absorbs one-off costs (the first run was often the
slowest in probes); the median ignores a run that lost a core to another
process. Assert that candidates agree before timing them. Numbers below come
from an Apple M3 Pro with 11 threads and change between renders; the prose
states only ratios that held in repeated runs. Interactively, `%timeit`.

### Row loops {#sec-perf-rows}

Miles per hour for every flight, as one expression and as three loops:

```{python}
def mph(distance: int, air_time: float | None) -> float | None:
    """The scalar version, for the loops."""
    return None if air_time is None else distance / air_time * 60


mph_native = flights_df.select(mph=pl.col("distance") / pl.col("air_time") * 60)["mph"]
two_cols_df = flights_df.select("distance", "air_time")
assert pl.Series("mph", [mph(*r) for r in two_cols_df.iter_rows()]).equals(mph_native)

race({
    "native expression": lambda: flights_df.select(pl.col("distance") / pl.col("air_time") * 60),
    "iter_rows(named=True)": lambda: [
        mph(r["distance"], r["air_time"]) for r in flights_df.iter_rows(named=True)
    ],
    "select(2 cols).iter_rows()": lambda: [mph(*r) for r in two_cols_df.iter_rows()],
    "zip(Series.to_list())": lambda: [
        mph(d, a) for d, a in zip(flights_df["distance"].to_list(), flights_df["air_time"].to_list())
    ],
}, runs=3)
```

The leanest loop is tens of times slower, named rows over a thousand. A
loop pays per row *and per column it is handed*: `iter_rows(named=True)`
builds a 19-key dict per flight (plain `iter_rows()`, a 19-value tuple,
measured ~1.5× faster). Selecting the two columns first cut it ten-fold, to
still more than a hundred times the expression; a `df.row(i)` loop was ~2×
slower again in probes. When the loop *is* the point (an API call or a
database insert per row, as in [Reading & Writing](io.qmd#sec-io-db)),
select the columns and iterate tuples. To compute a column, there is no fast
loop.

### Per-group loops {#sec-perf-groups}

Mean delay per group, by iterating a `group_by()` (≈ `group_split() |>
map()`) and natively, for keys with 3, 105 and 4,044 groups:

```{python}
def loop_mean(key: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """One Python iteration per group."""
    return pl.DataFrame(
        [{key: k, "avg_delay": sub_df["dep_delay"].mean()} for (k,), sub_df in flights_df.group_by(key)]
    )


def native_mean(key: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return flights_df.group_by(key).agg(avg_delay=pl.col("dep_delay").mean())


assert_frame_equal(loop_mean("tailnum"), native_mean("tailnum"), check_row_order=False)
pl.DataFrame([
    {"key": key, "groups": flights_df[key].n_unique(),
     "x_native": bench(lambda: loop_mean(key), 3) / bench(lambda: native_mean(key), 3)}
    for key in ["origin", "dest", "tailnum"]
]).with_columns(pl.col("x_native").round(0))
```

The native time barely moves with the group count; the loop pays tens of
microseconds per group (gather a sub-frame, call Python, build a dict): a
few times native for 3 groups, tens of times for 4,044. Per-group mutates
behaved alike in probes: `partition_by()` + loop + `pl.concat()`, and
`map_groups()` slower still, against one `.over()`. Loop only when each
group must leave Polars (a model fit, a file);
[Grouping](../transform/group-agg.qmd#sec-grp-escape) has native forms of
common per-group functions.

### Growing a frame {#sec-perf-grow}

1,000 pieces, as from 1,000 files or API pages, stacked three ways:

```{python}
piece_dfs = [flights_df.slice(i * 337, 337) for i in range(1_000)]


def concat_in_loop(dfs: list[pl.DataFrame]) -> pl.DataFrame:   # ≈ out <- rbind(out, piece)
    out_df = dfs[0]
    for piece_df in dfs[1:]:
        out_df = pl.concat([out_df, piece_df])
    return out_df


def extend_in_loop(dfs: list[pl.DataFrame]) -> pl.DataFrame:   # appends into out_df's buffers
    out_df = dfs[0].clone()
    for piece_df in dfs[1:]:
        out_df.extend(piece_df)
    return out_df


assert concat_in_loop(piece_dfs).equals(extend_in_loop(piece_dfs))
race({
    "concat(list) once": lambda: pl.concat(piece_dfs),
    "extend() in loop": lambda: extend_in_loop(piece_dfs),
    "concat() in loop, 500": lambda: concat_in_loop(piece_dfs[:500]),
    "concat() in loop, 1,000": lambda: concat_in_loop(piece_dfs),
}, runs=3)
```

`pl.concat()` copies no data (`rechunk=False` is the 2.0 default): each
result column is the list of its inputs' chunks. In a loop, call *i* copies
*i* chunk pointers per column, so the cost is quadratic in pieces, not rows:
doubling the pieces more than tripled the time, and 1,000 cost about a
hundred times one `pl.concat()`. `vstack()` in a loop measured the same;
`rechunk=True` inside the loop also copies the data (R's `rbind()` loop) and
was ~2.5× slower again. `extend()` stays linear with one chunk; its
docstring's advice, `vstack()` then one `rechunk()`, measured far slower for
1,000 small appends.

### Chunks and `rechunk()` {#sec-perf-chunks}

```{python}
flights_df_chunked = pl.concat(piece_dfs)
flights_df_rechunked = flights_df_chunked.rechunk()
chunk_ops = {
    "filter": lambda df: df.filter(pl.col("dep_delay") > 60),
    "with_columns": lambda df: df.with_columns(mph=pl.col("distance") / pl.col("air_time") * 60),
    "group_by().agg()": lambda df: df.group_by("dest").agg(pl.col("dep_delay").mean()),
    "sort": lambda df: df.sort("dep_delay"),
}
print("chunks in:", flights_df_chunked.n_chunks(), "vs", flights_df_rechunked.n_chunks(),
      "| a lazy collect():", flights_df.lazy().filter(pl.col("dep_delay") > 0).collect().n_chunks())
pl.DataFrame([
    {"operation": name,
     "x_slower": bench(lambda: op(flights_df_chunked)) / bench(lambda: op(flights_df_rechunked)),
     "chunks_out": op(flights_df_chunked).n_chunks()}
    for name, op in chunk_ops.items()
]).with_columns(pl.col("x_slower").round(1))
```

Element-wise steps run chunk by chunk and pass the chunking on, so the
overhead recurs at every later step; sorting and grouping write fresh
buffers. In probes, 11 chunks cost at most 1.5×, 100 about 2×, 10,000
60–160× on element-wise steps, and `rechunk()` (one copy) cost less than one
filter on the 1,000-chunk frame. A few chunks are normal in 2.0: `collect()`
returns one per engine batch (11 here), `read_csv()` gave 68 for the flights
CSV, `read_parquet()` one per row group. Rechunk once after assembling many
pieces, not after every read (2.0 removed the readers' `rechunk=`). One
chunk and no nulls is also what zero-copy `to_numpy(allow_copy=False)` needs
([Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-sharing)).

### Many `with_columns()` calls {#sec-perf-with-columns}

Merging every new column into one call is common advice. Eagerly, four
calls instead of one cost 1.2–1.4× in probes: columns computed earlier are
shared, not copied, so a call costs overhead and the parallelism across
expressions, nothing more. Lazily, the `cluster_with_columns` optimization
merges calls that don't depend on each other:

```{python}
print(
    flights_df.lazy()
    .with_columns(mph=pl.col("distance") / pl.col("air_time") * 60)
    .with_columns(gain=pl.col("dep_delay") - pl.col("arr_delay"))
    .with_columns(fast=pl.col("mph") > 500)
    .explain()
)
```

`mph` and `gain` share one `WITH_COLUMNS`; `fast` reads `mph`, so it stays a
separate step. Split steps for readability (`.pipe()` functions are plain
calls); in a lazy pipeline the optimizer merges what it can.

### Sorted flags {#sec-perf-sorted}

Every Series carries `flags`. `sort()` sets one; arithmetic, even `+ 0`,
clears it. Same values, with and without the flag:

```{python}
delay_sorted = flights_df["dep_delay"].drop_nulls().sort()
delay_plain = delay_sorted + 0          # same values, flag dropped
print(delay_sorted.flags, delay_plain.flags)

flag_ops = {"sort()": pl.Series.sort, "max()": pl.Series.max,
            "median()": pl.Series.median, "is_sorted()": pl.Series.is_sorted}
{name: round(bench(lambda: op(delay_plain), 9) / bench(lambda: op(delay_sorted), 9))
 for name, op in flag_ops.items()}
```

| Sets the flag | Keeps it | Drops it |
|---|---|---|
| `sort()`, `with_row_index()`, `pl.int_range()`, `set_sorted()` | `filter()`, `head()`, `drop_nulls()` | arithmetic, `cast()`, `fill_null()`, `pl.concat()`, a Parquet / IPC / CSV round trip |

: Verified on Polars 2.0.0 {.striped}

With the flag these become lookups: `sort()` returns its input, `max()` the
last value, `median()` the middle one. The saving is small in absolute terms,
since sorting data already in order is fast anyway (~6× faster than shuffled
in probes). In probes a flag also let `filter()` binary-search (8× on 10
million sorted integers, nothing on `flights`) and sped up joins (~2×);
`group_by()` gained nothing, and lost 2× with a million distinct keys.
`join_asof()`, `group_by_dynamic()` and `rolling()` check sortedness from the
data (a fast O(n) scan), so a flag only skips the check. `setkey()` is
`sort()`; prefer it to setting the flag by hand (@sec-perf-sorted-lie).

### Threads {#sec-perf-threads}

`pl.thread_pool_size()` is 11 here: one pool per process, sized to the
cores. `POLARS_MAX_THREADS` sets it, but only before `import polars`;
setting it later changes nothing (checked). So compare in fresh
interpreters:

```{python}
THREAD_PROBE = """
import json, statistics, timeit
import polars as pl
from pl_notes import datasets
flights_df = datasets.flights()
route = pl.col("origin") + "-" + pl.col("dest")
ops = {
    "sort": lambda: flights_df.sort("dep_delay", "arr_delay"),
    "group_by().agg()": lambda: flights_df.group_by("tailnum").agg(pl.col("dep_delay").mean()),
    "one string expression, eager": lambda: flights_df.select(route),
    "same expression, lazy": lambda: flights_df.lazy().select(route).collect(),
}
print(json.dumps({k: statistics.median(timeit.repeat(f, number=1, repeat=8)) for k, f in ops.items()}))
"""


def probe_secs(extra_env: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Run THREAD_PROBE in a fresh interpreter, which reads POLARS_MAX_THREADS at import."""
    probe = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", THREAD_PROBE], env=os.environ | extra_env,
                           capture_output=True, text=True)
    return json.loads(probe.stdout)


one_thread, all_threads = probe_secs({"POLARS_MAX_THREADS": "1"}), probe_secs({})
{name: round(one_thread[name] / all_threads[name], 1) for name in one_thread}   # speed-up from 11 threads
```

Sorting and grouping scale, far from 11×. The eager string expression did
not speed up at all: the eager context evaluated it as one task over the
column (several expressions in one context do run in parallel: six sped up
~2.4× in a probe). The streaming engine split the same column into batches
across threads. For one heavy element-wise step (strings, parsing, regex) on
a big column, `df.lazy()…collect()` is the parallel version.

Python-level parallelism adds nothing: queries in a Python thread pool share
the one Polars pool, and `map_elements()` holds the GIL (four threads gave no
gain in a probe). Run independent queries with `pl.collect_all()`
([Lazy API](lazy.qmd#sec-lazy-recipes)). With `multiprocessing`, use
`get_context("spawn")`: a `fork`ed child inherits Polars' locks without its
threads and can deadlock. `spawn` is the default on macOS and Windows; Linux
defaulted to `fork` before Python 3.14.

### Profiling a query {#sec-perf-profile}

```{python}
#| error: true
flights_df.lazy().profile()
```

| Tool | Shows | Runs the query? |
|---|---|---|
| `lf.explain()` | the optimized logical plan ([Lazy API](lazy.qmd#sec-lazy-explain)) | no |
| `lf.show_graph(plan_stage="physical", raw_output=True)` | the streaming operators as DOT text; the legend marks in-memory fallbacks | no |
| `pl.Config.set_verbose(True)`, `POLARS_VERBOSE=1` | engine decisions, scan details, scheduler state, on stderr | yes: a log firehose |
| `POLARS_LOG_METRICS=1` | per streaming operator: CPU time, rows in and out; per query: wall and CPU time | yes |
| `cProfile`, `%prun` | time spent in Python (UDFs, loops) | yes |

: Profiling tools in 2.0 {.striped}

`POLARS_LOG_METRICS` is not in the Python API docs (found in the 2.0
runtime); it is read per query and writes long lines to stderr. This helper
captures and parses them:

```{python}
def node_times(lf: pl.LazyFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """CPU time and row counts per streaming operator for one collect()."""
    with tempfile.TemporaryFile("w+") as log:
        saved_stderr = os.dup(2)
        os.dup2(log.fileno(), 2)                 # the engine writes to file descriptor 2
        os.environ["POLARS_LOG_METRICS"] = "1"
        try:
            lf.collect(engine="streaming")
        finally:
            del os.environ["POLARS_LOG_METRICS"]
            os.dup2(saved_stderr, 2)
            os.close(saved_stderr)
        log.seek(0)
        text = log.read()
    print(*re.findall(r"^Streaming query took .*?\)", text, re.M), sep="\n")
    to_ms = {"ns": 1e-6, "µs": 1e-3, "ms": 1.0, "s": 1e3}
    node_line = r"^(\S+): tot\(([\d.]+)(ns|µs|ms|s)\).*?recv\(row=(\d+).*?sent\(row=(\d+)"
    return pl.DataFrame(
        [(node, float(t) * to_ms[unit], int(n_in), int(n_out))
         for node, t, unit, n_in, n_out in re.findall(node_line, text, re.M)],
        schema=["node", "cpu_ms", "rows_in", "rows_out"], orient="row",
    ).sort("cpu_ms", descending=True)


node_times(
    flights_df.lazy().filter(pl.col("origin") == "JFK")
    .group_by("tailnum").agg(pl.col("dep_delay").mean()).sort("tailnum")
)
```

`cpu_ms` sums over threads: the nodes add up to the query's CPU time, not
its wall time. Operators run concurrently, which is why `profile()`'s
per-node wall clock was dropped. Read it as *where the CPU went* and *how
many rows each step saw*. The filter is a node here because the source is in
memory; on a Parquet scan with the filter pushed down there is no filter
node and the scan sends only the 111,279 JFK rows, while a `map_batches()`
before the filter made it send all 336,776 (a probe). Work the streaming
engine can't do shows as one `in-memory-map` node. The format is internal
and may change.

## Where it bites {#sec-perf-gotchas}

| Expectation | Polars 2.0 |
|---|---|
| a loop over groups is always slow | its cost is per group: 3 are fine, thousands are not (@sec-perf-groups) |
| `pl.concat()` copies nothing, so a loop of them is cheap | each call copies the chunk lists: quadratic in pieces (@sec-perf-grow) |
| chunk count is an internal detail | thousands of chunks slow every later element-wise step (@sec-perf-chunks) |
| `read_csv(..., rechunk=True)` from older tutorials | `ArgumentRemovedError`; call `.rechunk()` on the result |
| `set_sorted()` is a hint | a promise; break it and results are silently wrong (@sec-perf-sorted-lie) |
| a sorted column stays flagged after a file round trip | Parquet, IPC and CSV readers return it unflagged |
| `to_pandas()` / `from_pandas()` just work | both need `pyarrow`; the NumPy route changes dtypes (@sec-perf-pandas) |
| an eager step uses every core | one element-wise expression runs as one task (@sec-perf-threads) |
| `POLARS_MAX_THREADS` can change in a running session | read once, at import |
| `lf.profile()` | removed in 2.0; use `POLARS_LOG_METRICS` (@sec-perf-profile) |

: The differences at a glance {.striped}

### A false `set_sorted()` is silently wrong {#sec-perf-sorted-lie}

`set_sorted()` checks nothing. Tell Polars `[3, 1, 2]` is sorted and every
operation that reads the flag trusts it:

```{python}
lie = pl.Series("x", [3, 1, 2]).set_sorted()
right_df = pl.DataFrame({"t": [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1], "v": ["f", "e", "d", "c", "b", "a"]})
{
    "sort()": lie.sort().to_list(),                                     # truth: [1, 2, 3]
    "min(), max()": (lie.min(), lie.max()),                             # (1, 3)
    "median()": lie.median(),                                           # 2.0
    "filter(x > 1)": lie.filter(lie > 1).to_list(),                     # [3, 2]
    "unique() of [1, 2, 1]": pl.Series([1, 2, 1]).set_sorted().unique().to_list(),   # [1, 2]
    "join_asof(t = 3)": pl.DataFrame({"t": [3]})
    .join_asof(right_df.with_columns(pl.col("t").set_sorted()), on="t")["v"].to_list(),   # ["c"]
}
```

Every answer is wrong, with no warning. A grouped `agg()` splits one key
into several groups; `rolling()` and `group_by_dynamic()` crash with a Rust
`PanicException` instead of their "not sorted" error. data.table's
`setattr(DT, "sorted", "x")` is the same trap. `sort()` is cheap on ordered
data (@sec-perf-sorted), sets the flag, and is never wrong.

### pandas round-trips {#sec-perf-pandas}

Both directions go through Arrow; this book's environment has no `pyarrow`:

```{python}
#| error: true
flights_df.to_pandas()
```

`pl.from_pandas()` raises too unless every column is NumPy-backed, and the
default string dtype of pandas 3 is not. The NumPy route works, at a price:

```{python}
times_df = flights_df.select("dep_time", "time_hour")
times_pd = pd.DataFrame({c: times_df[c].to_numpy() for c in times_df.columns})
times_df_back = pl.from_pandas(times_pd)

print(times_pd.dtypes.astype(str).to_dict())
pl.concat([times_df, times_df_back.select(pl.all().name.suffix("_back"))], how="horizontal").head(1)
```

An integer column with nulls becomes `float64` with `NaN` (`nan_to_null=True`
restores the nulls on the way back, not the dtype), and the time zone is
dropped, leaving UTC wall-clock times. Even then, a round trip for one
grouped mean was ~6–8× slower than `.over()` in probes. Convert once, at the
edge of the pipeline, with `pyarrow` installed.

## Recipes {#sec-perf-recipes}

**Anti-pattern → replacement**, across the book:

| Anti-pattern | Replacement | Details |
|---|---|---|
| `for row in df.iter_rows()` to compute a column | one expression | @sec-perf-rows |
| `map_elements(lambda …)` | a native expression; `map_batches()` for a vectorised function | [Programming](../program/programming.qmd#sec-prog-udf) |
| `map_elements()` on a List column | `list.*`, `list.eval()` | [Nested Data](../types/nested.qmd#sec-nest-map-elements) |
| `for key, sub_df in df.group_by(...)`, `map_groups()` | `group_by().agg()`, `.over()` | @sec-perf-groups, [Grouping](../transform/group-agg.qmd#sec-grp-escape) |
| `pl.concat([out_df, piece_df])` in a loop | a list, then one `pl.concat()` | @sec-perf-grow |
| thousands of chunks | `rechunk()` once | @sec-perf-chunks |
| `read_*()`, then filter and select | `scan_*()` … `collect()` | [Lazy API](lazy.qmd#sec-lazy-measured) |
| `collect()` in the middle of a pipeline | one plan, one `collect()` | [Lazy API](lazy.qmd#sec-lazy-when) |
| several `collect()`s on one input | `pl.collect_all()` | [Lazy API](lazy.qmd#sec-lazy-recipes) |
| `String` keys sorted, grouped or joined repeatedly | `Enum` / `Categorical`, cast once | [Categorical](../types/categorical.qmd#sec-cat-why) |
| default `Int64` / `Float64` on a big frame | `shrink_dtype()`, narrower casts | [Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-recipes) |
| `maintain_order=True` everywhere, by habit | only where order is observed | [Grouping](../transform/group-agg.qmd#sec-grp-order), [Verbs](../transform/verbs.qmd#sec-verb-ties) |
| `set_sorted()` to skip a sort | `sort()` | @sec-perf-sorted-lie |
| `to_pandas()` mid-pipeline | stay in Polars; convert once at the edge | @sec-perf-pandas |
| one heavy element-wise expression, eager | `df.lazy()…collect()` | @sec-perf-threads |
| a Python thread or process pool around queries | `pl.collect_all()`; `spawn` if you must | @sec-perf-threads |

: Anti-patterns and replacements {.striped}

**Find the slow step of a query**: `node_times(lf)` (@sec-perf-profile). After
a file scan, a filter node that receives far more rows than it keeps is a
pushdown that didn't happen, often a UDF in the way
([Lazy API](lazy.qmd#sec-lazy-optimizations)).
